title: Wonder and the Unknown
objectives: I can use ten words to describe curiosity, mystery, and wonder.
I can tell the difference between a hunch, a riddle, and an enigma.
I can show how a character moves from being baffled to unraveling a mystery.
I can write about something that fills me with awe or curiosity.
rationale: Curiosity drives fifth-grade science and reading, but students often describe it with only interesting or weird. These ten words name the stages of wonder: the feeling (marvel, awe, fascinate, intrigue), the puzzle (enigma, riddle, baffle), and the thinking (ponder, hunch, unravel). They help students write about their own thinking and about unsolved questions in literature and science. The passage is an original mystery that moves in the same order as the words: wonder, puzzlement, a hunch, and a solved riddle. Ominous, reminisce, and nostalgia are revisited because mystery and memory both depend on mood, and because the end of a mystery can bring the same warm, thoughtful feeling as looking back.

words.def: To feel or show great wonder or surprise at something.
words.ex: We stopped on the trail to marvel at the huge waterfall.
words.ex2: Visitors marvel at the size of the whale skeleton in the museum.
words.nonExample: Yawning at a boring movie is not to marvel at it.

apps.academic: Scientists marvel at how a tiny seed can grow into a huge tree.
apps.spoken: I marvel at how fast she can read.
apps.writing: Use marvel with at to show wonder about a specific thing.

cloze.s: From the top of the hill, the hikers stopped to ___ at the valley glowing in the sunrise.

cloze2.s: The children could only ___ at the magician as he pulled a long scarf out of his tiny hat.

misuse.s: She was bored by the fireworks and began to marvel at how dull they were.
misuse.why: To marvel is to feel wonder; being bored is the opposite.

visual.alt: A shooting star above a surprised face.

words.def: To hold someone's attention with great interest.
words.ex: Bugs fascinate my little brother, so he can watch ants for an hour.
words.ex2: The old map of the harbor continued to fascinate the class all week.
words.nonExample: A dull list of rules does not fascinate most students.

apps.academic: Stories about the deep ocean fascinate many young scientists.
apps.writing: Use fascinate when something holds your attention strongly, not briefly.

cloze.s: Stories about space and distant planets ___ Tomas, who reads about them every night.

cloze2.s: The glowing jellyfish seemed to ___ the visitors, who stayed for the entire show.

misuse.s: The dull lecture was so boring that it began to fascinate everyone in the room.
misuse.why: To fascinate is to hold attention with great interest; a boring lecture does not.

visual.alt: A telescope and two eyes looking up.

words.def: To confuse someone so much that they cannot understand.
words.ex: The strange code began to baffle even the best students in the class.
words.ex2: Her sudden silence baffled the teacher, who had expected a loud argument.
words.nonExample: An easy question does not baffle anyone.

apps.academic: A baffling result may lead scientists to test a new idea.
apps.writing: Use baffle when something confuses someone so much they cannot find the answer.

cloze.s: The locked room and the missing book began to ___ the detective, who had no clue to follow.

cloze2.s: The complicated directions seemed to ___ everyone, and the group stood in the street, lost.

misuse.s: The simple question baffled no one, since everyone knew the answer at once.
misuse.why: To baffle is to confuse someone completely; a simple, clear question does not.

visual.alt: A face with a spinning head and a question mark.

words.def: To think carefully and for a long time about something.
words.ex: The chess player sat quietly to ponder her next move.
words.ex2: Before the big test, Luis liked to ponder each question before writing anything.
words.nonExample: Blurting out a quick answer is not to ponder.

apps.academic: Philosophers ponder big questions such as what makes something fair.
apps.writing: Use ponder for slow, careful thought, often about a big question.

cloze.s: On the long ride home, Rosa sat by the window to ___ what the old woman had said.

cloze2.s: The judge took a quiet minute to ___ the facts before announcing the decision.

misuse.s: He pondered the question for a quick half second and shouted the first answer he thought of.
misuse.why: To ponder is to think long and carefully, not to answer in half a second.

visual.alt: A thinking face with a thought bubble.

words.frame: I would ponder ___ if I had time.

words.def: Something puzzling and hard to understand; a mystery.
words.ex: The missing treasure remained an enigma for a hundred years.
words.ex2: To his friends, the quiet new boy was an enigma, because he never said where he had lived before.
words.nonExample: A question with an obvious answer is not an enigma.

apps.academic: Scientists still call some parts of the deep ocean an enigma because we know so little.
apps.spoken: The ending of that book is an enigma.
apps.writing: Use enigma for a puzzling person, thing, or event that is hard to explain.

cloze.s: How the ancient builders moved the giant stones remains an ___ that no one has fully explained.

cloze2.s: The detective said the case was an ___, since every clue seemed to point in a different direction.

misuse.s: The sunny weather was an enigma, since everyone clearly knew why it was warm.
misuse.why: An enigma is puzzling and hard to explain; a fact everyone knows is not.

visual.alt: A question mark on a locked box.

words.frame: An enigma I would like to solve is ___.

words.def: To untangle something, or to solve a mystery bit by bit.
words.ex: Detectives work step by step to unravel the mystery of the stolen painting.
words.ex2: The kitten pulled one thread and began to unravel the whole sweater.
words.nonExample: Tying a knot is the opposite of unraveling one.

morph.note: Ravel can mean either to tangle or to untangle, which is why unravel is the clearer word.

apps.academic: Historians unravel a mystery by comparing clues from many documents.
apps.spoken: I tried to unravel the knot in my shoelace.
apps.writing: Use unravel for untangling thread or working out a mystery step by step.

cloze.s: Using only the footprints and a torn note, the detective began to ___ the puzzle of the missing key.

cloze2.s: With a patient hand, Ava tried to ___ the knotted yarn without breaking a single thread.

misuse.s: To unravel the sweater, she tied every thread into a tighter knot.
misuse.why: To unravel is to untangle; tying tighter knots does the opposite.

visual.alt: A ball of yarn with a loose thread.

words.frame: To unravel a mystery, I would ___.

words.def: To make someone very curious about something.
words.ex: The odd noise in the attic began to intrigue the twins.
words.ex2: Ancient maps with missing corners intrigue her, and she studies them for hours.
words.nonExample: A shopping list does not intrigue most people.

apps.academic: Strange patterns in nature intrigue scientists and lead them to ask questions.
apps.writing: Use intrigue as a verb for making someone curious, usually about something mysterious.

cloze.s: The locked door at the end of the hall began to ___ the whole class, who wondered what was inside.

cloze2.s: The unusual shape of the shell seemed to ___ Marcus, who studied it for an hour.

misuse.s: The plain gray poster intrigued everyone, and no one felt even a little curious.
misuse.why: To intrigue is to make people curious; if no one feels curious, the poster did not intrigue them.

visual.alt: A detective holding a magnifying glass.

words.def: A feeling of wonder, mixed with respect or a little fear.
words.ex: The campers sat in awe as the northern lights rippled across the sky.
words.ex2: She looked at the towering redwoods with awe.
words.nonExample: Feeling bored by a long speech is not awe.

apps.academic: Many explorers describe awe when they first see the polar ice.
apps.spoken: I felt awe at the size of the canyon.
apps.writing: Use awe for a deep feeling of wonder, not for something that is only fun.

cloze.s: The children stood in ___ as the huge whale rose slowly out of the water beside the boat.

cloze2.s: As the thunder rolled across the valley, the hikers watched the storm in silent ___.

misuse.s: She felt awe when she yawned during the dull meeting.
misuse.why: Awe is a deep feeling of wonder; yawning with boredom is not awe.

visual.alt: A starry sky above a small open-mouthed face.

words.def: A feeling that something is true, without proof.
words.ex: I had a hunch that it would rain, so I packed an umbrella.
words.ex2: The detective followed a hunch and found the missing key in the garden.
words.nonExample: A fact you have measured and checked is not a hunch.

apps.academic: A scientist may begin with a hunch and then test it with an experiment.
apps.spoken: I have a hunch she'll be late.
apps.writing: Use hunch for a feeling that you cannot prove yet.

cloze.s: Without any proof, Dani had a ___ that her brother had hidden the last cookie.

cloze2.s: The coach had a ___ that the quiet new player would become the team's best scorer.

misuse.s: His hunch was a proven fact that he had measured three times with a ruler.
misuse.why: A hunch is a feeling without proof; a measured fact is not a hunch.

words.def: A puzzling question or saying with a clever, hidden answer.
words.ex: The first riddle asked what has hands but cannot clap, and the answer was a clock.
words.ex2: Grandpa told a riddle at dinner, and no one could guess the answer.
words.nonExample: A plain question with an easy, direct answer is not a riddle.

apps.academic: A riddle uses clever words to hide its answer from the listener.
apps.writing: Use riddle for a word puzzle with a hidden answer.

cloze.s: The librarian asked a ___ about something with pages and a spine, and the students guessed a book.

cloze2.s: It took the class ten minutes to solve the ___ that the teacher had written on the board.

misuse.s: The riddle told us the answer in plain words right at the start.
misuse.why: A riddle hides its answer in clever words; stating it plainly is not a riddle.

visual.alt: A puzzle piece beside a question mark.

passage.title: The Bell That Would Not Ring
paras: Behind the school garden, Zoe found a brass bell half buried in the soil. When she shook it, it made no sound at all. She began to marvel at the tiny letters that circled its rim, a pattern she had never seen. "This is an enigma," said her friend Kofi, who loved big words. "A mystery with no answer yet."

The bell fascinated them both, and soon it began to baffle them. The letters made no words in English. "I have a hunch," said Zoe. "Maybe it's a riddle." Kofi stood and pondered the idea for a long minute. Then he copied the letters onto thin paper, turned it over, and held it to the window.

The mystery began to unravel. Read from the back, the letters spelled, "Look where the sun sleeps." The words intrigued them even more. At sunset, they stood by the garden fence and watched the sun slide behind the old oak. Beneath its roots lay a small tin box. Inside was a metal clapper, the part that makes a bell ring.

Zoe fitted the clapper inside the bell and swung it gently. A deep, clear note rolled across the garden. The two friends stood in awe. "Some riddles," Kofi said softly, "are meant to be solved with a friend."

qs.q: In paragraph 2, the word "baffle" most nearly means
qs.why: The letters made no words in English, so the bell began to confuse the friends, which is what baffle means.

qs.q: What does Kofi mean when he calls the bell an enigma?
choices: It is a mystery with no answer yet.
It is too heavy to lift.
qs.why: Kofi explains that an enigma is a mystery with no answer yet.

qs.q: How did Kofi read the hidden message?
choices: He read it aloud at sunset.
He asked the teacher for help.
He copied the letters onto thin paper and held it to the window from the back.
He looked at the bell in a mirror.
qs.why: The text says he copied the letters onto thin paper, turned it over, and held it to the window, and then the message could be read from the back.

qs.q: Why did the friends go to the garden fence at sunset?
choices: To ring the bell for dinner.
To follow the clue about where the sun sleeps.
To find a place to hide the bell.
qs.why: The message told them to look where the sun sleeps, so they watched where the sun sets and found the box under the oak.

qs.q: Which sentence best states the main idea of the passage?
choices: Garden fences are good for hiding things.
Curiosity and teamwork can turn a puzzling mystery into a solution.
Letters are easier to read from the back.
qs.why: Zoe and Kofi follow their curiosity, work through the puzzle together, and solve it, and Kofi says riddles are meant to be solved with a friend.

teacher.overview: Students learn ten words for curiosity and puzzles: marvel, awe, fascinate, and intrigue for the feeling; enigma, riddle, and baffle for the puzzle; and ponder, hunch, and unravel for the thinking. The passage is an original mystery that follows the same order. Writing and discussion ask students to describe their own wonder and to tell how they work through something puzzling.

notes.va.marvel.v: Marvel as a verb means to feel wonder at something, and it is usually followed by at. Students may know Marvel as a brand name; clarify the verb sense. Ask what they have marveled at this week.
notes.va.fascinate.v: Fascinate means to hold your interest strongly. It is stronger than interest. Students often say the fascinating thing for any interesting item; push for what exactly holds the attention.
notes.va.baffle.v: Baffle means to confuse so much that you cannot find a way through. It is stronger than confuse. Link to puzzles and mazes. Students can role-play a baffled face before they write.
notes.va.ponder.v: Ponder means to think about something carefully and for a long time. It suggests quiet thought, not a quick answer. Ask students to name a question they would like to ponder over a weekend.
notes.va.enigma.n: An enigma is a puzzling person, thing, or situation. The adjective is enigmatic. Students may confuse it with enema or other words; slow pronunciation helps (ih-NIG-muh). Ask which famous mysteries are enigmas.
notes.va.unravel.v: Unravel has a literal sense, to untangle thread, and an extended sense, to solve a puzzle by working out its parts. The passage uses the second. Bring a tangled string and untangle it as a model for solving a mystery.
notes.va.intrigue.v: As a verb, intrigue means to make someone very curious. The noun means a secret plan, as in political intrigue. Teach the verb here. Note that the verb is stronger than interest and often hints at mystery.
notes.va.awe.n: Awe is a feeling of wonder with respect, sometimes with a little fear. It is a noun, and the adjective is awestruck. Students may use awesome casually; the unit asks them to use awe when the feeling is deep, as before a vast view.
notes.va.hunch.n: A hunch is a feeling that something is true, without proof. It is not a fact or a guess made at random. Contrast with proof and evidence from the argument unit. Ask students how a hunch can lead to a test.
notes.va.riddle.n: A riddle is a puzzling question or statement whose answer is hidden in clever words. It differs from an enigma, which is a puzzle in life or nature. Have students write a simple riddle and ask a classmate to solve it.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'Zoe says she has a hunch that the letters are a riddle. She has no proof yet, only a feeling. Kofi stops to ponder, which means he thinks for a long time. When the message appears, the mystery begins to unravel, like a knot coming loose. Each word names a different step in solving the puzzle.'

A hunch is a proven fact.

extend: Write a riddle for the class to solve and a one-sentence clue that does not give the answer.

teacher.reviewAdvice: Revisit ominous, reminisce, and nostalgia by asking how an ominous mood can add to a mystery, whether a character who solves a mystery might reminisce about it later, and how nostalgia differs from wonder. Return to the ten words after two days, again at one week, in a mystery story.

frames: I have a hunch that ___ because ___.
wida.oral: Partner A describes something puzzling or amazing without naming the word. Partner B names the matching word from the unit, such as awe, riddle, or hunch, and says one more detail.

needsReview: Spanish glosses not reviewed by a native speaker: maravillarse (marvel), desconcertar (baffle), reflexionar (ponder), desentrañar (unravel), asombro (awe), corazonada (hunch), adivinanza (riddle).

Teacher note for unravel says ravel can mean either to tangle or to untangle; this is a standard dictionary observation but was not checked against a cited dictionary. Teacher note says intrigue as a noun means a secret plan.
Reading letters from the back of thin paper works only when the writing is made to be read in mirror image; the passage presents it as a clue, not a fact about all writing.
